explanation: Foster's hypothesis says otter damage ultimately makes eelgrass meadows healthier. If meadows elsewhere get less healthy the longer otters have lived there and the larger the otter population is, that directly contradicts the idea that otter activity benefits meadow health. Choice B is tempting, but sites with otters and no eelgrass at all say nothing about whether otter damage helps existing meadows.

The text says bees use nonhexagonal cells to fill gaps, and the gap problem gets worse as the size difference between worker and drone cells grows. The graph shows the western honeybee uses far fewer nonhexagonal cells (under 0.5% of each type) than the other two species (over 2%), so its worker and drone cells are probably closer in size. Choice D gets the direction wrong: fewer nonhexagonal cells means a higher, not lower, percentage of hexagonal cells.

The text explains that New Mexico's isolation kept its colonists from hearing later changes to Spanish, so the dialect kept older features. That shows how geographical isolation can shape the way a language develops. Choice B is too broad; the passage is about why one dialect changed less, not about change in every generation.

The passage says off-off-Broadway theaters freed artists to experiment, then introduces Fornés as "one such artist" who could stage her plays exactly as she wanted. She is therefore an example of the artistic opportunity these theaters offered. Nothing in the text discusses costs, relative complexity of staging, or how famous she might have been.

The text praises the book as comprehensive, unique and valuable, then names one shortcoming: it lacks a unifying authorial point of view. Choice D captures both halves. Choice A is tempting, but the flaw described is a missing point of view, not missing information about key events.

The text says HILDA is expensive because it needs years of data collection. The fitness study is described as a contrast, so it can be cheap because it doesn't need years of data collection. Choice A says the opposite, and choices B and C talk about HILDA instead of the fitness study.

Richard admits he started the trouble ("I do the wrong"), says he himself has "cast" Clarence "in darkness," and pretends to weep about it while blaming the queen and her allies. So he fakes grief and shifts blame while actually causing the king's hostility. Choice A misses that his grief is fake and that he caused the problem; choice B wrongly calls Derby, Hastings and Buckingham the queen's allies.

Day's features look fit for a bust or a stamp, and he seems obviously brainy, yet the narrator jokes that it would be rude to ask what he actually achieved, and even his memoirs bury that information. So he looks distinguished, but whether he accomplished anything is unclear. Choice B goes too far: nothing says his memoirs reveal dishonorable acts.

The researchers think the lava released nitrate into the water. The table supports a lava connection: in both depth ranges, nitrate was far higher in the lava-affected area (3.1 and 0.4) than outside it (0.03 or less and 0.01 or less). Choice A is about phosphate, which isn't the nutrient in question, and choice C compares nitrate to phosphate, which says nothing about the lava's effect.

The text's main point is that the researchers concluded the 41 settlements were culturally linked to Izapa, partly because they share its layout (pyramid to the north, plaza to the south). Choice A reverses the relationship, and choice C focuses on when the settlements were found rather than on what the researchers concluded.

Black-furred wolves are more common where distemper outbreaks are frequent, and they are more likely to be immune. Together this suggests the gene variant for black fur may be connected to distemper immunity. Choice D overreaches; the findings actually favor black-furred wolves in some areas, not their replacement.

Taller corn can grow more ears but is more likely to snap or be uprooted by wind before harvest. Shorter corn avoids that risk, so more of it may survive to harvest, which could actually raise yields. Choice B contradicts the text, which links uprooting to greater height.

If some artifacts are from the 1200s but the settlement wasn't founded until the 1300s, the artifacts must have been made somewhere else and later brought to Kuulo Kataa, for example through trade or migration. Choice C is tempting, but the founders' origin wouldn't explain why objects are older than the settlement itself.

The surprise would be a result that doesn't fit expectations. Broccoli is a nonmycorrhizal species that shouldn't benefit from the fungi, yet it averaged slightly more mass with the fungi (7.5 g) than without (7 g). Choice C is true but expected, since marigolds are mycorrhizal hosts.

The text says Indigenous languages hold knowledge about medicinal plants in their vocabulary, and that this knowledge is at risk as the languages fade. Keeping the languages in use therefore also preserves that knowledge. Choice B is wrong because the goal is keeping the Indigenous languages alive, not moving their terms into English.

The claim is that the narrator was frightened of the sailor. Choice D shows that fear directly: the sailor "haunted" his dreams and appeared to him with "a thousand diabolical expressions." The other quotations describe the sailor's arrival, habits or clothing but show no fear.

The first sentence states the main idea: initiatives that rely on natural features or processes can help with conservation. The logjam project is just an example of that idea. Choice C is a detail from the example, and choice D overstates the text by claiming nature-based methods are better than all others.

The map's ink contains titanium dioxide, which wasn't used in ink until the early 1900s, so the map couldn't have been drawn in the mid-1400s. Choice A goes too far: showing the map is fake doesn't prove that no Europeans of that era knew about North America.

The text describes how the popular, affordable bicycle let people live farther from work, visit nearby towns, take up new sports and form clubs, all new opportunities. Choice C is only one detail, and choices B and D (preferred travel method, safety) are never discussed.

Whistler waves have been recorded on Venus, but the same missions saw few other signs of lightning, such as flashes. That leads to the idea that something other than lightning, perhaps a feature of Venus that Earth lacks, is producing the waves. Choice B is too extreme, since nothing suggests the waves aren't real whistler waves, and choice A has no basis because the text never questions the data's precision.

Lutie notices how nice the street looks in the sunset glow and watches children playing ball, tag and double dutch. She is observing the street at a particular time of day and what is happening on it. She isn't annoyed, puzzled or hiding from her neighbors.

The researchers say moved items make shoppers walk through more of the store and buy things they hadn't planned on. In choice A, the shopper's cleaning supplies had been moved, and while searching, she spotted and bought a notebook. Choice B involves moved items but no unplanned purchase, and choice C is about an obvious cue (a coupon).

The conclusion is that the venom reduces a risk during feeding, namely infection by E. coli. If E. coli is often found in the scorpion's prey and survives its digestive juices, then eating prey really is risky, and venom that kills E. coli would help. Choice A weakens the conclusion by suggesting E. coli poses no threat to the scorpion.

The researchers changed only the timing of downbeats and offbeats, and listeners were far more likely to say the changed versions had swing. That suggests this timing plays an important role in creating swing. Choice A is wrong because both changes were made together, so the effect of offbeats alone can't be isolated.

Even though no one can read the Indus script, artifacts have revealed the civilization's customs and organization. So knowing a civilization's language isn't required to learn about it. Choice A goes too far by calling research easier without the language, and choice D contradicts the text, since the script remains undeciphered.

Daughters matched their mothers' diets for two years after separation but not by year five, which points to a social learning effect that fades. Cousins were no more similar than unrelated bears, which argues against genetics, while the modest similarity among unrelated bears in similar habitats means environment can't be ruled out. Choice D wrongly gives genetics a significant role, and choice C wrongly dismisses social learning.

The oldest Acasta rocks (4.02 bya) look like plume rocks, but rocks from 3.75 bya resemble modern subduction rocks. So subduction-like processes were happening in at least some places by 3.75 bya. Choice B gets the timing wrong, since 4.02 bya rocks show a plume setting, not subduction.

Only TEXES (2007, 2019) and VISIR (2006) provided spectroscopy data, so the earliest spectroscopy came from VISIR at the European Southern Observatory in 2006. Choice D is tempting because 2003 is earlier, but the LWS data were infrared imaging, not spectroscopy.

A higher manganese-to-calcium ratio means lower oxygen. In the Alboran Sea, the ratio jumps from about 33 at 10,000 years ago to about 83 at 8,000 years ago, a big oxygen drop around the coral's decline 9,000 years ago. Near the Mauritanian coast the ratio stays nearly flat (about 12 to 19) throughout, including around 11,000 years ago. Choice A reverses the Alboran trend.

Stern and Gerya argue that Earth's shift to plate tectonics sped up the evolution of complex life and that tectonics could narrow the search beyond the usual criteria. So among habitable-zone planets with atmospheres, those with plate tectonics are better candidates. Choice D is wrong because they add tectonics as a further filter rather than ranking it above orbit or atmosphere.

The researcher needs a lake whose ice duration dropped between 1980–81 and 2005–06. Oulujärvi went from about 195 days of ice to about 155 days, a clear decline. Choice B is wrong because Lake Neusiedl's ice days increased, and choices A and D each describe only one winter, so they can't show a decline.

The text says Karenin "hated change" and that dog time moves in a circle, following the same path day after day; even moving a flower pot disturbed him. So his sense of time makes him prefer predictability and dislike disruption. Choice B is unsupported because the text doesn't say his reaction grew stronger after the move, and choice C wrongly gives Tomas and Tereza the same circular sense of time.

The researchers concluded that sediment entered these streams from many spread-out places, so there was no single source for distance to be measured from. If stream banks regularly collapse into the water at multiple points upstream of the sampling sites, sediment is indeed entering from many locations. Choice D is tempting, but tributaries entering downstream of the sampling sites couldn't affect the sediment that was sampled.

On the graph, Algeria's urban share starts at about 40% in 1970 and rises to about 74% in 2020, so it went from around 40% to more than 70%. Choice C describes Nigeria's line, not Algeria's, and choices A and B don't match Algeria's values.

The text says that in 2017 Favela made a life-size, piñata-like sculpture of the Gypsy Rose lowrider car, which was shown at the Petersen Automotive Museum. Jesse Valadez is mentioned only as the car's famous driver, not as the subject of a sculpture.

The student claims review emotionality has nothing to do with box office success. If higher emotionality scores predicted higher box office earnings, the two would clearly be related, which weakens that claim. Choices A and D involve star ratings instead of linking emotionality to box office results.

Jasmonic acid defends against herbivores and salicylic acid against microbes. Plants exposed to air from whitefly-free plants made more jasmonic acid than controls (about 205 vs. 140), but plants exposed to air from infested plants made less jasmonic acid (about 100) and more salicylic acid (about 175 vs. 120). That shift toward microbial defense is exactly what the conclusion describes. Choice D leaves out the salicylic acid increase that shows the plants favoring microbial defense.

The text says Izquierdo was important and her work is high quality, yet she is little known in the US because Kahlo and Rivera attract so much attention. Choice A sums this up. The other choices bring in claims about gallery displays, subjects, techniques or how many works she made, none of which the text discusses.

The claim is that the setting where Valia reads is nearly silent. Choice D says the room was so quiet that the only sound was the rustling of pages, which directly shows that. Choice B mentions his reading but says nothing about quiet.

The word "Yet" signals a surprise about the Navajo-Churro, which is described as coarser overall. The table shows its inner fibers can be as thin as 10 microns, finer than the mouflon's 15 and the Merino's minimum of 17, so at its softest, its inner fiber is softer than both. Choice D is wrong because the Navajo-Churro's inner fiber can be as thick as 35 microns, coarser than the mouflon's 15.

The shortcoming described is that corporations can keep their agreements with communities confidential. If the agreements are secret, outsiders can't check whether the communities are being paid fairly, which undercuts the protocol's purpose. Choices A and B describe effects that confidentiality wouldn't cause.

The traditional view says voting doesn't change attitudes toward candidates. If people who voted later held more polarized attitudes toward the winner than similar people who were too young to vote, voting itself appears to have changed their attitudes. Choice A suggests attitudes depend on political orientation regardless of voting, which supports rather than weakens the traditional view.

High pressure compresses water by destabilizing its hydrogen bonds. If those bonds stay more stable under high pressure when TMAO is present, TMAO is helping water resist compression, just as the hypothesis says. Choice C would show the opposite (more TMAO, faster compression), and choice B is about TMAO's own shape, not water's.

The hypothesis depends on a chain: fewer sharks means more cownose rays, which means more oysters get eaten. Finding that rays increased as sharks decreased confirms the key middle link. Choice C points the other way, since oyster consumption rising before the shark decline would suggest the sharks weren't the cause.
In the table, the lemons row under the July 2021 column shows $31.78 per box. Choice D ($28.94) is the June 2021 lemon price, and choices B and C are grapefruit prices.
The table lists the 1984 World's Fair as costing $350 million with 7.35 million visitors. The other numbers belong to the 1962, 1968 and 1974 fairs.

In choice C, Lear strikes his own head and blames it for letting his "folly" in and his "dear judgement" out, which shows he regrets his actions. Choice A does the opposite, presenting himself as more wronged than wrong, and choice D is a threat of revenge, not regret.

Paredes argued that Mexican American folklore comes mainly from ongoing interactions among cultures in Mexico and the US, not from colonial Spain. If most of the collected folklore was clearly recent corridos about history and social life, it couldn't have been inherited from Spanish rule, which supports Paredes. Choice A supports Espinosa instead, since the décima originated in Spain.

The tablet suggests Merneith was in charge of the treasury and other central offices. Whether or not she was a pharaoh, that means she had an important role in Egypt's government. Nothing in the text supports claims about her travels, a new writing system, or when she lived relative to the First Dynasty.

The claim says Wheatley speaks directly to Virtue and asks for help reaching a future goal. In choice A she addresses Virtue ("Attend me, Virtue") and asks it to "guide my steps to endless life and bliss," a future goal. Choice D addresses her own soul rather than Virtue, and choices B and C don't ask for help reaching a goal.

The text says conventional ETL fabrication can waste up to 80% of the solution, raising costs at scale, and that spray coating may avoid this problem. So the conventional method is likely less suitable for large-scale manufacturing than spray coating may be. Choices B and C compare it to other architectures or approaches that the text never discusses.

The text says disco is widely ridiculed as superficial, notes that its love-and-heartbreak themes are "hardly unique to disco," and argues its songs also address deeper concerns. That suggests disco has been unfairly dismissed for subject matter other genres share. Choice A is wrong because the text says scholars have defended the genre, not ignored it.

The appendix evolved independently many times and didn't disappear once it appeared, and species with it have more immune-supporting lymphoid tissue. Together these suggest it has been kept because it helps the immune system. Choice C makes an unsupported prediction about the future, and choice A is about nonmammals, which weren't studied.

Walsh found that users became aware of how their listening looked to others and changed their behavior because of it. The user in choice A picks songs that followers might like instead of what they actually want to hear, which is exactly that. Choice C mentions the social side but shows no change in listening behavior.

The critics point out that even though the trees were grown specially for the project, it's too early to know whether they can thrive on the building. In other words, it's unclear whether Bosco Verticale can support its plant life. The other choices raise concerns the text never mentions.

The graph shows the lowest-performing spray-coated ETL at about 15.5% efficiency, higher than the best spin-coated ETL at about 13.5%. So even the worst spray coating beat the best spin coating, strong evidence for the conclusion. Choice C has the wrong values (the best spray result is about 17%), and choice D compares only spray-coated layers.

The text focuses on a gray seal spitting water at an eagle, a behavior never seen in seals before, plus a biologist's ideas about why. Bird-watching and eagles are only part of the setting, not the main topic.

Mulvey says conspicuous editing and a lack of point-of-view shots lead viewers to take a more critical stance toward the protagonist. The attic scene has both, so by her logic it should weaken viewers' identification with the protagonist. Choice A is backward, since conspicuous editing would make viewers more aware of the artifice, not less.

The songs describe terraced clam gardens, and archaeological evidence shows clams got bigger and more plentiful when that method was in use. This supports the idea that the ancestral practice both kept up the clam supply and made it stronger. Choice C is unsupported because the text gives no archaeological comparison with Sakha or Kaluli songs.

The only negative effect value in the table, -0.6254, belongs to the common dandelion as the neighboring species. Virginia spring beauty and Himalayan balsam have positive values, and star chickweed is a target species, not a neighbor.

In choice D, the speaker hears birdsong in a grove and is in a mood where "pleasant thoughts / Bring sad thoughts to the mind," so he feels both pleasure and sadness at once. The other quotations describe only the pleasure of nature, with no contradictory feeling.

The text says each novel is unique and the product of its own circumstances, so guessing how it would have turned out if typed is mere speculation. It follows that there's no reasonable way to evaluate how a work would differ if written another way. The other choices make claims about efficiency, success or speed that the text never supports.

The example should contrast the same element (iron) in slower AST dust with faster HTC or OCC dust. Iron's ablation rate is 28% in AST dust but 90% in HTC dust, illustrating the claim. Choice A compares two slow sources, and choices B and D switch to sodium, which isn't a same-material comparison.

Gibson decorates punching bags with beadwork, leather fringe and jingles, traditional Native art forms, to make new original works. The text doesn't say he designs dresses (C), discuss non-Native influences (B), or mention color and pattern (D).

In September, Rincón, Ponce and Isabela all fall around 6 to 6.5 inches, below 8, while San Sebastián is about 11 inches, above 8. Choice A is wrong because San Sebastián gets more rain than Rincón, and in choice D Ponce (about 6 inches) is not similar to San Sebastián.

The narrator calls himself humble and slovenly but stresses that he knew "a truly great man," spent years at his side, and watched his genius at work. The main idea is his appreciation for the long time he spent with someone he admired. Choice D focuses on one detail about the inventor rather than the narrator's main point.

Since engulfed water grows with body length faster than baleen area does, longer whales should take longer to filter. Fin whales (18–22 m) take about 31 seconds, much longer than minke whales (7–10 m) at about 9 seconds. Choice D is wrong because blue whales do not have the most lunges per dive; minke whales do.
From 1910 to 1925, cars produced rose from 123,990 to 3,185,881, while companies producing cars fell from 320 to 80. Only choice A describes production rising and the number of companies falling.

Neither the striped burrowing frog nor the dainty green tree frog produces bufadienolide, yet the tadpoles ate 10% of the former's eggs but only 1% of the latter's. Since bufadienolide can't explain that difference, something else must also affect egg preference. Choice C fits the bufadienolide explanation rather than challenging it.

The table shows Eris (Dysnomia) and Makemake (MK 2) each have exactly one moon. Haumea has two moons, Pluto has five and Ceres has none, so every other choice includes a dwarf planet that doesn't fit.

The puzzle is how a snake gene could reach frogs, since frogs rarely survive snake encounters. If parasites that feed on both snakes and frogs also carry BovB, they offer a plausible indirect route for the gene to pass from snakes to frogs. Choice A only explains spread among frogs, not how the gene got from snakes to frogs in the first place.

The cost savings from digital technology were biggest in manufacturing and distribution, which come after writing, editing and design. So the costs of those earlier stages were affected less by the technology. The other choices make claims about long works, customer expectations or print runs that the text doesn't address.

The researchers argue that Europa's ridges formed the same way as a similar pair in Greenland, with a subsurface ocean playing the role that surface water plays on Earth. Choice A captures both points. Choice D is wrong because the text offers an explanation (the subsurface ocean) rather than saying researchers are stumped.

The team predicts that females' preference for their own subspecies' sound will push the two subspecies further apart over time. If the migratory males' feather sound becomes more and more different in pitch over generations, that is the kind of growing divergence the hypothesis predicts. Choice D points the other way, suggesting the subspecies are staying the same, and choice A is about flight rather than mating.

Henry admits his mild temper ("smooth as oil, soft as young down") let the nobles trample on his patience and cost him their respect, and he vows to be his true self from now on, "mighty and to be fear'd." Choice C is the reverse: he says he will abandon his calm disposition, not keep it.
The text directly states the flower bud was found in a 164-million-year-old fossil. The numbers 145 and 201 million are the boundaries of the Jurassic period, not the fossil's age.

The period eye calls for studying how artworks were understood in their own time. If many art historians since the 1970s have focused on exactly that, the approach has clearly influenced the field. Choice D describes work done before Baxandall, so it can't show his influence, and choice A suggests historians rejected a key part of his idea.

The text says Aspera will observe the "warm-hot" CGM gas, which hasn't been observable before and likely fuels star formation, to help explain how galaxies evolve. Choice D states this main point. Choice B is only background, and choice A wrongly claims Vargas will be the first to study the CGM at all.

Yellowstone's line is the highest in June (about 940,000), July (about 1,080,000) and August (about 920,000). Rocky Mountain comes second in July and August, and in June it ties with Zion well below Yellowstone.

In choice B, the speaker watches workers "sadly shuffle on" at dawn in New York and then says he would rather be "on the island of the sea," setting his feelings about the city against his longing for home. The other choices describe only one place, so they can't show contrasting feelings.
